title: AI chips explained: why Nvidia, Broadcom and Intel react so differently to the same news
body: Key takeaways: The AI chip industry has three layers: general-purpose chips, custom chips and manufacturing. General-purpose chipmakers like Nvidia benefit most from broad AI demand. Custom chip designers like Broadcom gain as big AI developers seek alternatives, but carry concentration and financing risks. Foundries need anchor customers to fill costly plants, which is why customer news moves Intel so sharply. Power supply, supplier diversification and concentrated manufacturing are shaping all three layers. GPUs, ASICs and foundries: a reader's guide to the AI chip race Why can one AI headline lift Nvidia to a record while knocking Intel lower on the same day? The answer is that "AI chips" is not a single business. Companies compete in different layers of the industry, each with its own economics, risks and drivers of success. Understanding those layers makes it much easier to read news from the sector and to see why investors react so differently to it. Key terms GPU (graphics processing unit): A general-purpose processor that can run many kinds of AI workloads. Nvidia's GPUs are the industry standard for training and running large AI models. ASIC (application-specific integrated circuit): A chip custom-designed for a particular customer or task. It is less flexible than a GPU but can be cheaper or more power-efficient for the job it was built for. TPU (tensor processing unit): Google's custom AI chip, an example of an ASIC, designed with Broadcom.

title: Why a few words from Elon Musk can (and did!) move a $600 billion+ chipmaker

Why a few words from Musk can move a $600 billion chipmaker: Intel and the Terafab test Intel shares fell on Monday after Elon Musk confirmed that Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC) is in talks about joining Terafab, the Texas chip venture backed by Tesla, SpaceX and xAI. title: BOJ may signal that inflation has hit 2% target, keeping December rate hike firmly in play
body: Even if there likely won't be another rate hike this month, the BOJ appears to be preparing to take another step towards further policy tightening. The latest report from Reuters notes that the BOJ could signal in its October quarterly outlook that underlying inflation has roughly reached its 2% target, according to sources familiar with the central bank's thinking. Now, that's quite significant from a symbolic sense. For a central bank that has spent years trying to generate sustainable inflation, that would mark a meaningful shift in the policy backdrop. And that underscores the readiness to raise interest rates again in the coming months. In other words, the shift is not a guarantee that rate hikes will follow but it does reinforce market expectations of a move in December and perhaps is a suggestion that the BOJ could even step up the pace of its policy tightening. The sources also point to steady wage gains alongside firmer consumer and wholesale inflation as reasons for the change in tone. title: Solana launches open settlement standard for institutions, with JPMorgan input
body: Solana launches open settlement standard for institutions: what JPMorgan's role actually means The Solana Foundation has launched Solana DvP, an open-source program designed to let banks and other financial institutions settle trades of tokenised assets on the Solana blockchain in a single step. The foundation announced it in New York on Monday, 5 October, and said JPMorgan provided input on institutional settlement practices during development. The headline link to JPMorgan is the part readers should look at most carefully. The program is new and potentially useful, but it is not yet evidence that big banks are moving trades onto Solana. What happened Solana DvP is an escrow program released under the MIT licence, which means anyone can use, adapt and build on it without paying licensing fees. It gives institutions a standard way to carry out delivery-versus-payment, or DvP, settlement on Solana. DvP is the basic safeguard of securities markets: the asset and the cash change hands at the same time, or the trade does not happen at all. That removes the risk of one side paying and the other failing to deliver. In traditional markets this runs through clearing houses, depositories and custodians, and typically takes one to two days. The foundation says its program does it in one atomic transaction, with finality in seconds.
